name: Adam Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for speaking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, independent of AI firms, employers, unions, political parties and government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential and your name won't be attached. What happens on an ordinary shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I answer breakdown and membership calls for a roadside service, mostly late afternoon into evening. A driver tells me the warning light, I check their cover, and I book a truck or explain why a claim is disputed. I left school after secondary education and have done this thirteen years; I'm experienced, not one of the technical specialists.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What keeps you there, and what does your household depend on?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like turning a panicked call into a clear plan, and the late rate pays better than most desks nearby. I use the approved AI search every day to find policy clauses, then read the actual membership record before promising a truck. My wife Mira works at a garden centre, our grown children pay their own way, and we have about ten months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the afternoon team that a faster policy search is fine if the truck still goes to the right road. A driver needs a truck at the right road, not a polished policy summary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My late shift seems secure in a mild change, and ten months saved gives Mira and me breathing room. I would still watch whether the company uses small time savings to stretch the same agents over more calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep handling breakdown calls and use the approved search against the membership record. In the first year of AI Plateau I would bring three mistaken search results to our team meeting, so nobody treats a summary as a booking authority.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my wage for now. I have enough saved to argue about a bad target without making it a household emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sort of search mistake have you seen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week a policy search said 'home start' when the driver had only roadside cover. The membership record settled it, not the neat paragraph on my screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend any of the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mira and I wouldn't spend the reserve on a newer car because the old one still runs. That money is for a period without work, not a reward for a convenient search box.

say: I would welcome **faster policy search** if a person checks the membership record.
I would tell agents **wrong bookings** still cost real time.
think: I expect my **late wage** to continue through a mild change.
I can question **tighter targets** because ten months saved gives us room.
do: Keep handling **breakdown calls** with approved search and original membership records.
Bring **three wrong search results** to a team meeting in the first year.
feel: I feel **calm** about wages and alert to poor summaries.
S0.quote: A driver needs a truck at the right road, not a polished policy summary.
fieldNote: His **daily AI use** is already part of ordinary roadside calls.
A **ten-month reserve** gives him room to challenge careless targets without risking the household budget.

steps.text: Keep handling breakdown calls using approved search against the original membership record
Bring three mistaken policy searches to the first-year team meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the desk that software will handle the easy renewals and breakdown questions, so we should ask what happens to the evening premium. I would rather see a paid rota than a promise that experienced agents are valued.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can handle disputes, but we may need fewer agents even on late calls. If the evening premium goes, my full week could lose enough pay to matter despite our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would learn the new AI dispatch checker by testing twenty closed breakdown bookings on paid shifts and listing every wrong location. In the first year routine calls move, I would compare the posted late rotas at nearby roadside desks; I would change only if written weekly wages and hours after travel replace what this desk pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the premium rather than the screen itself. I can test software, but I cannot make a company keep an expensive shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a failed test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wrong location means the truck drives to the wrong end of town. I would compare the checker with the actual dispatch record before anyone uses it on a live stranded driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your savings cover a lower rate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mira's garden-centre wage helps, but it would not replace my late rate. Ten months saved lets us refuse a lower-paid transfer, not ignore the difference forever.

say: I would ask for **written evening hours** as routine calls move.
I would tell colleagues **wrong dispatch locations** need checking against actual records.
think: I could lose my **evening premium** even if I keep harder claims.
Our **ten-month reserve** cannot replace that weekly wage indefinitely.
do: Test **twenty old bookings** with the new AI checker on paid shifts and record wrong locations.
Compare **posted late rotas** after routine calls move; change only for written after-travel wages and hours matching current pay.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a lower paid week, while able to test the tool.
S1.quote: Ten months saved lets us refuse a lower-paid transfer, not ignore the difference forever.
fieldNote: His **late premium** matters more than an improved search screen.
A new job requires **written weekly terms** after travel, including the evening premium he currently earns.

steps.text: Test twenty closed breakdown bookings with the new AI dispatch checker during paid shifts
Compare posted nearby late rotas once routine calls move
Change desks only for written after-travel weekly wages and hours matching current pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI by 2028 could settle roadside claims cheaper than we do, while hands-on robots arrive around 2031. The mechanic's work has a little longer; the call desk does not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my evening desk could lose most of its calls before a new schedule is ready. We have ten months saved and several nearby centres, so I can search, but I will not pretend Mira's wage alone pays our whole household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would put the last three late-shift pay slips beside our household bills and ask dispatch what paid human exceptions it expects to retain. If most of my desk hours end in the first year after 2028, I would apply for posted paid dispatch jobs nearby; I would accept only written full-week wages and hours covering bills after the journey, while keeping any paid calls still offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing most of my own evening income, though I have some room to look. A reserve buys time, not another working week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask dispatch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask how many live drivers still need a person when the screen says no cover. If dispatch keeps that work, I need the paid hours in writing, not a picture of a new department.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children help cover the gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children have their own bills, and I will not put their wages into ours. Mira and I can use savings for a search if the cuts arrive, but we would first see exactly how much the late rate has disappeared.

say: I would say **2028 thinking AI** hits claims before 2031 repair robots.
I would ask for **paid human exceptions**, not a new-department picture.
think: I expect **most evening calls** might end quickly.
I have **ten months saved** for a search, but my wife's wage cannot replace mine.
do: Compare **three late-shift slips** with bills and ask dispatch for its paid exception hours.
Apply after **2028 hours end** for posted paid dispatch work; accept only written after-journey weekly wages and hours covering bills.
feel: I feel **alarmed** at the possible loss of most of my evening income.
S2.quote: A reserve buys time, not another working week.
fieldNote: Strong savings offer **search time**, while the expected call loss remains large.
He would keep **paid calls** until a posted role has written bill-covering weekly terms.

steps.text: Keep any paid roadside calls and request written dispatch exception hours
If most hours end after 2028, apply for posted paid local dispatch jobs
Accept only written full-week wages and hours covering bills after travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends the 2031 date gives a worker time to see a real vacancy before handing in notice. Thinking AI will reach bookings then, while workshop robots are a later matter around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could work these five years and keep the reserve intact if the late rate holds. I am good with callers but average at dispatch rules, so I would not take over a workshop or buy a van merely because machines are coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would ask the local roadside depot for one paid shift watching its human dispatch desk, if a place is available. If my calls shrink in the first year after 2031, I would apply for a posted paid dispatch role only when the written weekly hours and wages after travel cover our bills; until then I would keep taking offered paid calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious that my own late rate could shrink, though five years lets me inspect a real shift. I won't buy an imagined future with the money Mira and I saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look for on that depot shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to see who talks to the stranded driver when the map is wrong, and who has authority to send a truck. Watching one paid shift would answer more than a course brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop working at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I cannot say I will retire at 63 just because there is a date on this card. Mira and I would check actual income statements and our bills before reducing either wage.

say: I would say **2031 AGI** changes bookings before 2034 workshop robots.
I would inspect a **real paid shift** before moving desks.
think: I might keep my **reserve intact** if the late rate lasts.
I cannot treat a **van purchase** or retirement date as a plan without numbers.
do: Ask for a **paid depot observation** in 2026 if a place is available.
Apply after **2031 call cuts** only for posted dispatch work with written after-travel weekly hours and wages covering bills.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a possible loss of my own late-rate income.
S3.quote: Watching one paid shift would answer more than a course brochure.
fieldNote: He wants to inspect **dispatch authority** before relying on a new role.
He rejects a speculative **van purchase** and an unchecked retirement date while preserving the savings cushion.

steps.text: Keep offered paid roadside calls while asking for a paid depot observation if available
After 2031 cuts, apply for posted paid dispatch with after-travel weekly wages and hours covering bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my brother a decade is useful if we keep earning and check what actually changes on the roadside desk. Full thinking AI reaches claims in 2036, with repair robots roughly 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may want fewer evenings, but I cannot name what income replaces that premium. Ten months saved is a cushion, not a wage that lasts year after year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mira and I would get our actual income statements and add up a year of household bills this winter. I would keep the late shift while it pays, check the posted local rotas every year, and decide on fewer evenings after 2036 only if verified income covers the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly uneasy; a decade gives us time for an honest calculation. I would rather keep a paid night than make a boast about retirement we cannot support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of your pay needs its own line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count the evening premium separately because a daytime wage might not replace it. If a local employer posts a better rota later, we can compare the full week instead of guessing now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children cover the gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children can visit for supper without paying our bills. I am not assuming a pension figure until Mira and I see it in an actual statement.

say: I would say **2036 claim AI** arrives before 2039 repair robots.
I would tell family a **decade** helps only while paid work continues.
think: I cannot name **replacement income** for the evening premium at 68.
I see **ten months saved** as a cushion, not a permanent wage.
do: Gather **actual income statements** with Mira and total a year of bills this winter.
Keep **paid late shifts** and compare posted rotas yearly; reduce evenings only if verified income covers the gap.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about later income, with time to check it.
S4.quote: Ten months saved is a cushion, not a wage that lasts year after year.
fieldNote: He treats a **retirement date** as conditional on actual replacement income.
His **higher evening rate** must be included when comparing future work or deciding to reduce paid hours.

steps.text: Keep paid late roadside calls while the current rota remains
Total a year of bills with Mira and check actual replacement income before reducing evening shifts
Compare posted local rotas yearly by full-week pay before changing jobs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because most of the paid evening calls could vanish before a depot has another seat. Written hours for human exceptions and a real posted dispatch opening would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the late premium separately from the job title. A daytime offer can sound equal until the weekly pay is counted.

headlineQuote: A daytime offer can sound equal until the weekly pay is counted.
portrait: A **58-year-old** experienced roadside caller with secondary-school education and average job skill.
He uses **approved AI daily** but verifies the original membership record.
His **higher late rate** and ten-month reserve support Mira and him; grown children have their own bills.
He tests **written weekly pay** before moving jobs or reducing evenings.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture could end most evening calls before another paid depot seat exists.
whatWouldHelp: Written **human exception hours** and a real posted dispatch opening would help.
